title: Gerald L. Clore and Jeffrey R. Huntsinger (2009) — How the Object of Affect Guides Its Impact; Emotion Review 1(1), 39–54; DOI 10.1177/1754073908097185
source_type: author-hosted theoretical review by an OCC coauthor and collaborator
why_retain: Readable PDF text extracted; relevant pp. 39–49 read on 2026-10-21. Strong accessible account connecting emotion objects with meaningful appraisals rather than label membership.
definition_support: The OCC Account of Emotions, p. 44: 'three kinds of targets for emotion: outcomes, actions, and objects'. Own paraphrase of source: event outcomes are evaluated relative to goals; actions relative to standards; object attributes relative to tastes/attitudes. Explicit account, not merely a list.
limits: Review of the 1988 OCC account, not direct inspection of the 1988 book or independent validation. Its object includes psychological situations, not only physical objects. This architecture remains source context, not required game-design categories. Subsystem and process proposals elsewhere in paper do not establish biological causes.

title: Clore and Huntsinger (2009) — How the Object of Affect Guides Its Impact; self/other action-appraisal observation
why_retain: Separate observation retained for achievement and other-directed distinction; same readable source, not an additional external URL.
definition_support: The OCC Account of Emotions, p. 44 explicitly characterizes pride, shame, admiration, and reproach as approval/disapproval of actions judged against standards, then distinguishes 'self (e.g., pride, shame) or other (e.g., admiration, reproach)'. Own paraphrase: action appraisal and whose action it is both matter.
limits: Exact within-account family meanings, not full lexical definitions or rules for every use of these words. Does not define naches or substantiate gratitude-versus-admiration from this passage. Do not treat pride as synonymous with any success or automatically equate admiration with benefit received.

title: Clore and Huntsinger (2009) — How the Object of Affect Guides Its Impact; threat/loss/object-appraisal observation
why_retain: Separate observation retained for threat, loss, aversion, and complex appraisals; directly readable prose, not just category labels.
definition_support: Outcome-focused Emotions–Fear and Anxiety, p. 45: 'displeasure about the prospect of an undesirable outcome of events'. Own paraphrase of adjacent subsections, pp. 45–46: sadness concerns undesirable outcomes relevant to goals; disgust concerns unappealing object attributes; anger combines an undesirable outcome with disapproval of the action seen as producing it.
limits: Fear and anxiety are grouped rather than exactly distinguished. Grief, homesickness, and loneliness appear as examples, not separately specified definitions. Experiments reviewed are not game-play findings. No warrant to infer emotion from behavior, prove a biological cause, or make these distinctions universal.

title: Clore and Huntsinger (2009) — How the Object of Affect Guides Its Impact; subtype-definition gap
why_retain: Negative observation prevents family-level coverage from being promoted into exact lexical support; source inspected on 2026-10-21.
definition_support: P. 44 names joy, sadness, hope, fear, disappointment, and relief as outcome-focused examples. Relevant inspected account does NOT specify the exact prospect-confirmation conditions for relief/disappointment or exact meanings of gratitude and regret.
limits: Listing terms is not defining them. This source cannot alone ground the requested disappointment/regret or gratitude/admiration distinctions. Search-generated OCC summary was not accepted as source evidence; in particular, do not silently substitute regret for remorse.

title: Klaus R. Scherer (2005) — What are emotions? And how can they be measured?; Social Science Information 44(4); DOI 10.1177/0539018405058216
why_retain: Official GEW page links this article; readable PDF text extracted and relevant sections through PDF p. 22 read on 2026-10-21. Primary conceptual account useful for appraisals and eliciting-event context.
definition_support: Event focus, printed p. 700, explicitly allows external events, one's own behavior, memories, and imagined events; Appraisal driven, p. 701: 'we do not generally get emotional about things or people we do not care about'. Own paraphrase: interpreted relevance to concerns, needs, desires, and goals matters in this account.
limits: Author's component-process proposal, not a universally accepted account or demonstrated neurological mechanism. No individual vocabulary definition follows from this general description. Source discusses body/subsystem theories; do not import these as proven biological causes. Printed PDF pagination differs from official landing-page citation; use DOI plus section and PDF-page locators.

title: Scherer (2005) — What are emotions? And how can they be measured?; related-experience boundary observation
why_retain: Separate observation retained for careful inclusion of related experiences without pretending all terms mean short emotion episodes.
definition_support: A component process definition of emotion and feeling, PDF pp. 3–5, and design-feature discussion, PDF pp. 9–12: explicit conceptual descriptions distinguish subjective feeling, mood, preference, attitude, affect disposition, and interpersonal stance. Own paraphrase: a word can denote an enduring tendency or an episode, so intended sense must be stated.
limits: These are Scherer's conceptual boundaries, not mandatory categories for the workbench. For example, his placement of enduring love as an attitude is a proposal, not a reason to exclude love-related experiences. Supports context/term-sense care, not a glossary of every emotion named.

title: Scherer (2005) — What are emotions? And how can they be measured?; vocabulary-list limitation
source_type: officially hosted theoretical article with coding-instrument discussion
why_retain: Separate observation records a tempting broad vocabulary lead and why its entries must not be mistaken for definitions.
definition_support: Exploring the semantic space of folk concepts of emotion, printed p. 707: 'How many emotions are there? I submit that there is currently no answer to this question.' Table 4, PDF pp. 20–21, supplies affect categories and word stems; following text, PDF p. 22, explains author-judged synonym/near-synonym/family grouping.
limits: Table 4 is a coding lexicon, not exact relational/appraisal definitions, equivalence proof, or validated universal taxonomy. Aesthetic-emotion examples likewise do not individually define every listed term. No full lexicon or instrument copied; do not use group membership to fill definition gaps.
